newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Reporters accuse Serbian authorities of censorship.
newsitem.headline: Reporters accuse Serbian authorities of censorship.

text.p: Reporters at Serbian newspapers on Thursday protested at what they say is a government attempt to gag reporting on a wave of opposition protests.
Fourty-one journalists walked out of the popular new independent daily Blic over what they said was the owner's capitulation to pressure from the Socialist government of President Slobodan Milosevic.

The paper had given front-page coverage to the wave of demonstrations which has jammed the streets of Belgrade daily since the authorities overturned clear opposition victories in local elections on November 17.
The deputy editor-in-chief Cvijetin Milivojevic resigned on Wednesday evening, citing a decision by the Austrian owner Peter Kelbel to slash the paper's political coverage.
"He prohibited any further mention of the demonstrations and demanded that our political events pages be cut back from four to just one," Milivojevic said.
The paper's foreign editor Vjekoslav Radovic said the journalists were convinced Kelbel had bent under political pressure.

"Until now he hasn't interfered in our editorial policy, and told us he was delighted with the way the paper was going. But then today he told us it was a disaster and wanted it changed," Radovic said.
"It is quite clear he has been leaned on. He is trying to save his investment by changing policy and keeping the paper ticking over."

Blic staff also accused the state-controlled printing works of trying to limit its circulation. The printers had pressed the paper to cut its circulation down from 200,000 to some 80,000 due to "technical difficulties".
Earlier, reporters from Belgrade's independent radio station B-92 said the authorities were jamming its reports of the demonstrations.
"Everything is okay as long as we broadcast music but as soon as we begin the news programme they start jamming us," journalist Aleksandar Vasovic said.
Marchers have hurled eggs and abuse at the offices of state broadcasters, widely regarded as instruments of president Slobodan Milosevic's power.

Journalists from the state-controlled newspaper Politika -- which has also been subjected to egg-attacks -- wrote to the paper's editorial board protesting its pro-government coverage of the demonstrations.
"We are not advocates of partial journalism but are for the respect of facts and events which are unfolding before the eyes of our readers," said the letter, a copy of which was faxed to Reuters.
A speaker at Thursday's rally read out a letter he said had come from a group of reporters at the state news agency Tanjug.

"We ask you today when you march through the city to pass by Tanjug as well," said the speaker quoting from the letter. "State TV and radio are reporting news (on the demonstrations) that Tanjug has published so we should not be spared."
